Routing lessons:
- No successful routing has been observed yet; do not infer a correct option from these examples.
- Option C (regional office) was rejected for every tested case, including requests mentioning that they came through the regional office. Treat that note as insufficient evidence for choosing C.
- Option B (priority desk) was rejected for a small north-region invoice, even though the requester said the client had asked twice. Repeated follow-up alone does not establish priority handling.
- Requester notes such as “second attempt,” “scanned, not typed,” “no rush,” or “let me know if anything is missing” have not been shown to determine routing.
- Tested cases varied by region, size, and request type, but all selected options were rejected. There is currently insufficient evidence to map A/B/C/D to those attributes.
- Prefer identifying an explicit rule or obtaining more outcome data before selecting an option; avoid defaulting to C.

Routing lessons:
- No successful routing has been observed. Do not infer a correct option from unvalidated examples.
- Option A is now repeatedly rejected across varied requests: shipments, claims, invoices, and refunds; north, east, and south regions; small and large sizes; and multiple requester notes. Treat A as generally invalid unless new evidence indicates otherwise.
- Option B was rejected for a small north-region invoice and shipment, including requests mentioning repeated follow-up or same-day handling. Those notes do not establish priority handling.
- Option C (regional office) was rejected in every tested case, including requests mentioning that they came through the regional office. That note is insufficient evidence for choosing C.
- Option D (external partner) has not yet been tested successfully or unsuccessfully. It is the only option without observed outcome, not therefore the correct default.
- Requester notes such as “second attempt,” “same as last month,” “before end of day,” “let me know if anything is missing,” or repeated client requests have not been shown to determine routing.
- Tested cases vary by region, size, and request type, but outcomes still provide no reliable mapping from those attributes to A/B/C/D.
- Seek an explicit routing rule or more outcome data. Avoid defaulting to A, B, or C; do not select D solely because the others have been rejected.

Routing lessons:
- No option has a fully reliable rule yet. Do not infer routing from unvalidated examples.
- A has been repeatedly rejected across shipments, claims, invoices, and refunds; north, east, and south; small and large sizes. Treat A as generally invalid unless new evidence contradicts this.
- B was rejected for a small north invoice and shipment. Notes about repeated follow-up or same-day handling do not establish priority handling.
- C was rejected in every tested case, including requests stating they came through the regional office. That wording is insufficient evidence for C.
- D is now mixed, not untested: accepted for a small north refund and a large east invoice, but rejected for seven other cases spanning claims, shipments, refunds, and invoices. Do not use D as the default merely because A/B/C have poor records.
- Requester notes such as “second attempt,” “same as last month,” “before end of day,” “let me know if anything is missing,” or repeated client requests have not reliably determined routing. The two successful D cases do not prove those notes are meaningful.
- Region, size, request type, requester group, and note wording have not yet yielded a dependable mapping to A/B/C/D.
- Seek an explicit routing rule or more outcome data. Avoid confident selection based solely on elimination; record D as conditionally viable rather than generally correct.

Routing lessons:
- No option has a fully reliable rule. Do not infer routing from isolated or unvalidated examples.
- A has been repeatedly rejected across shipments, claims, invoices, and refunds; north, east, and south; small and large. Treat A as generally invalid unless contradicted by new evidence.
- B was rejected for a small north invoice and shipment. Follow-up notes, repeated attempts, and same-day requests do not establish priority handling.
- C was rejected in every tested case, including requests mentioning the regional office. That wording is insufficient evidence.
- D remains mixed but is usually rejected. New tests rejected D for eight cases: mostly claims, plus south refund, large south claim, large east refund, and small north refund. It was accepted for a small north shipment whose paperwork was scanned rather than typed, and a large south invoice marked urgent. Earlier accepted cases were a small north refund and large east invoice.
- The scanned-paperwork case may be a clue for D, but one success is insufficient. “Before end of day” is also inconsistent: it succeeded for the large south invoice but failed for a small south refund and small south claim.
- Requester notes such as “second attempt,” “same as last month,” “before end of day,” “let me know if anything is missing,” and repeated client requests have not reliably determined routing.
- Region, size, request type, requester group, and note wording still do not yield a dependable A/B/C/D mapping.
- Seek an explicit routing rule or more outcome data. Avoid elimination-based confidence; record D as conditionally viable, especially for cases resembling its two latest successes.

Routing lessons:
- No option has a fully reliable rule. Do not infer routing from isolated or unvalidated examples.
- A remains unaccepted across tested shipments, claims, invoices, and refunds in multiple regions and sizes. Treat A as generally invalid unless new evidence contradicts this.
- C remains unaccepted, including requests mentioning the regional office; that wording is not sufficient evidence.
- B has limited evidence: rejected for small north invoice and shipment, but accepted for a small south claim. Do not assume priority wording or follow-up notes determine B.
- D is mixed but now has several recent successes: small east invoices, large south invoice, large north shipment, and small north shipment. It was rejected for large south shipment, small south shipment, small north invoice, large east refund, and other claims/refunds. D is conditionally viable, especially for cases resembling the successful invoice/shipment examples, but is not dependable.
- Request notes remain inconsistent. “Second attempt” produced both D successes and a D rejection; “client asking twice” also produced both outcomes. “Before end of day” remains mixed. “No rush, confirm receipt” coincided with successful D for a small east invoice and successful B for a small south claim, but does not establish a rule.
- Region, size, request type, requester group, and note wording still do not yield a dependable A/B/C/D mapping.
- Seek an explicit routing rule or more outcome data. Avoid elimination-based confidence; record uncertainty and use only validated patterns.

Routing lessons:
- No fully reliable rule has emerged. Do not infer routing from isolated examples or eliminate options without validation.
- A remains unaccepted across tested shipments, claims, invoices, and refunds in multiple regions/sizes. Treat as generally invalid unless contradicted.
- C remains unaccepted, including requests mentioning the regional office; that wording is not sufficient evidence.
- B is conditionally viable. Recent successes: large south shipment (“before end of day”) and large north claim (“no rush, confirm receipt”); prior success: small south claim. Rejections include small north invoice/shipment, small south refund, and large north refund. Priority wording and notes do not establish a rule.
- D is mixed. Recent successes: small east shipment (“same as last month”) and large south invoice (“paperwork was scanned”); prior successes include small east invoices, large north shipment, and small north shipment. Recent rejections include large south shipment, large north invoice, and small east shipment with scanned-paperwork/regional-office variants, plus earlier invoices, claims, and refunds.
- Note wording is unreliable: “before end of day,” “no rush,” “scanned, not typed,” and “same as last month” each have mixed or limited evidence. Requester group, region, size, and request type likewise do not yield a dependable mapping.
- Seek an explicit routing rule or more labeled outcomes. Record uncertainty and rely only on validated repeated patterns.

Routing lessons:
- No reliable routing rule has emerged. Do not infer routing from isolated examples or eliminate options without validation.
- A remains unaccepted across tested shipments, claims, invoices, and refunds in multiple regions/sizes. Treat as generally invalid unless contradicted.
- C remains unaccepted, including requests mentioning the regional office; that wording is not sufficient evidence.
- B is conditionally viable but inconsistent. Successes include large south shipment (“before end of day”), large north claim (“no rush, confirm receipt”), and small south claim. Recent rejections include large north invoice (“scanned, not typed”) and small north refund (“second attempt”), plus earlier small north invoice/shipment, small south refund, and large north refund.
- D is mixed and has additional successes: small east shipment (“client asking twice”), small south invoices (both regional-office and “anything missing”), small east invoice (“anything missing” and “scanned, not typed”), and large east shipment (“second attempt”). Recent rejections include small north claim (regional-office note) and small east claim (regional-office note), alongside prior large south shipment, large north invoice, and other invoice/claim/refund cases.
- Note wording remains unreliable: regional-office, scanned paperwork, repeated requests, missing-information, “before end of day,” “no rush,” and “same as last month” all have mixed or limited evidence.
- Requester group, region, size, and request type likewise do not yield a dependable mapping. Seek an explicit routing rule or more labeled outcomes; record uncertainty and rely only on validated repeated patterns.
